reminder: A Stein manifold is a [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold) with enough [holomorphic functions](c:holomorphic-function) to separate points and give local coordinates.
definition: A Stein manifold is a [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold) $X$ that is holomorphically convex and whose [holomorphic functions](c:holomorphic-function) separate points and give local coordinates. Holomorphically convex means that for every [compact](c:compact-space) set $K$, the hull of $K$ is compact; the hull is the set of points $x$ with $|f(x)|\le\sup_K|f|$ for every holomorphic $f$ on $X$. Equivalently, $X$ is a closed complex submanifold of some $\mathbb{C}^N$.
examples: The space $\mathbb{C}^n$ is Stein, because its coordinate functions already separate points.
Every open subset of $\mathbb{C}$ is a Stein manifold.
The smooth affine curve $y^2=x^3-x$ is a closed complex submanifold of $\mathbb{C}^2$, so it is Stein.
Non-example: The projective line $\mathbb{CP}^1$ is not Stein, because every holomorphic function on it is constant.

steps: Start with a [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold) $X$ and its holomorphic functions.
Require that the holomorphic functions separate points and give local coordinates.
Require that the hull of every compact set is compact.
A complex manifold with both properties is a Stein manifold.
links.why: Every Stein manifold is a complex manifold, so all results on complex manifolds apply; the two extra conditions are what make Stein manifolds special.

reminder: A subalgebra is a subset of an [algebra](c:algebra-over-a-field) that contains $1$ and is closed under sums, products and scalar multiples.
definition: Let $A$ be an [algebra over a field](c:algebra-over-a-field) $K$. A [subset](c:subset) $B\subseteq A$ is a subalgebra when $1\in B$ and $B$ is closed under addition, multiplication and multiplication by scalars of $K$. Then $B$ is itself an algebra, with the operations of $A$.
examples: The polynomial functions form a subalgebra of the algebra of continuous functions $[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}$.
The upper triangular $n\times n$ matrices form a subalgebra of the matrix algebra $M_n(K)$.
The scalar multiples of the identity matrix form a subalgebra of $M_n(K)$.
Non-example: The strictly upper triangular matrices are closed under sums, products and scalars, but they do not contain the identity matrix.

steps: Regard the algebra $A$ as a ring.
A [subring](c:subring) contains $1$ and is closed under sums, differences and products.
A subalgebra is a subring that is also closed under multiplication by scalars of $K$.
links.why: It shows the one extra condition that a subalgebra adds to a subring: closure under scalar multiplication.

steps: Take a dense subalgebra $B$ of a topological algebra $A$.
Forget density, which is a condition on the topology.
What remains is a subset that contains $1$ and is closed under the algebra operations, so $B$ is a subalgebra.
links.why: Every fact about subalgebras holds for a dense subalgebra; density is only an extra topological condition.

reminder: A surjection is a [function](c:function) in which every element of the codomain is the output of some input.
definition: A [function](c:function) $f:A\to B$ is a surjection when for every $b\in B$ there is some $a\in A$ with $f(a)=b$. Equivalently, the [image](c:image) $f(A)$ equals the codomain $B$.
examples: The map $x\mapsto x^3$ from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{R}$ is a surjection.
The projection $\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}$, $(x,y)\mapsto x$, is a surjection.
The quotient map $\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ is a surjection.
Non-example: The map $x\mapsto x^2$ from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{R}$ is not a surjection, because no input gives $-1$.

steps: Start with any [function](c:function) $f:A\to B$.
Compute its image $f(A)$, the set of all outputs.
Add the condition $f(A)=B$.
links.why: A surjection is a function with one extra condition, so every fact about functions applies to it.

steps: A [bijection](c:bijection) $f:A\to B$ has an inverse function $g:B\to A$.
For each $b\in B$, the element $g(b)$ is an input with $f(g(b))=b$.
So every bijection is a surjection, and it is also injective.
links.why: Bijections are exactly the surjections that are also injections.

reminder: The Todd class is the multiplicative [characteristic class](c:characteristic-class) of complex bundles given by $x/(1-e^{-x})$ in the Chern roots.
definition: Let $E$ be a [complex vector bundle](c:complex-vector-bundle) of rank $r$ with formal Chern roots $x_1,\dots,x_r$, so that the [Chern classes](c:chern-class) $c_i(E)$ are the elementary symmetric polynomials in the $x_i$. The Todd class is $\mathrm{td}(E)=\prod_{i=1}^{r}x_i/(1-e^{-x_i})$, a symmetric power series in the roots and hence a series in the Chern classes. It is multiplicative: $\mathrm{td}(E\oplus F)=\mathrm{td}(E)\,\mathrm{td}(F)$.
examples: For a line bundle $L$ with $c_1(L)=x$, the Todd class is $1+x/2+x^2/12+\cdots$.
A trivial bundle has Todd class $1$.
For a complex manifold $X$, the Todd class $\mathrm{td}(X)$ is that of its tangent bundle; for $\mathbb{CP}^1$ it is $1+[\mathrm{pt}]$.
Non-example: The total Chern class $\prod_i(1+x_i)$ is also multiplicative, but it uses the series $1+x$, not $x/(1-e^{-x})$.

steps: Write the Chern roots $x_i$ of a complex bundle $E$ formally.
The product $\prod_i x_i/(1-e^{-x_i})$ is a symmetric series in the $x_i$.
A symmetric series in the roots is a series in the [Chern classes](c:chern-class) of $E$.
Chern classes are natural under pullback, so this series is a natural class of bundles, a characteristic class.
links.why: The Todd class is one characteristic class, fixed by one power series in the Chern roots.

reminder: The trace of a [square matrix](c:square-matrix) is the sum of its diagonal entries.
definition: For a [square matrix](c:square-matrix) $A=(a_{ij})$ of size $n$, the trace is $\operatorname{tr}A=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{ii}$, the [sum](c:sum) of the diagonal entries. Over an algebraically closed field, it equals the sum of the [eigenvalues](c:eigenvalue) of $A$, counted with multiplicity. It satisfies $\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)$.
examples: The $n\times n$ identity matrix has trace $n$.
The matrix with rows $(1,2)$ and $(3,4)$ has trace $1+4=5$.
A rotation of the plane by the angle $\theta$ has trace $2\cos\theta$, the sum of its eigenvalues $e^{i\theta}$ and $e^{-i\theta}$.
Non-example: A $2\times3$ matrix has no trace, because it is not square.

steps: Finite-dimensional vector spaces form a symmetric monoidal category in which every object is dualizable.
A square matrix $A$ is an endomorphism of $K^n$.
The [categorical trace](c:categorical-trace) of $A$ is the composite of coevaluation, $A$, a swap and evaluation.
In the standard basis, this composite is the number $\sum_i a_{ii}$.
links.why: The matrix trace is the categorical trace in the category of vector spaces, so the same idea defines traces in other settings.

reminder: A triangular number is a number of the form $1+2+\cdots+n$, which equals $n(n+1)/2$.
definition: For a [natural number](c:natural-number) $n$, the $n$-th triangular number is $T_n=1+2+\cdots+n=n(n+1)/2$, the [sum](c:sum) of the first $n$ positive integers. It counts the dots in a triangle that has $n$ dots in its bottom row.
examples: The first triangular numbers are $1,3,6,10,15,21$.
The number $10$ is triangular: $10=1+2+3+4$, and ten bowling pins form a triangle with rows of $4$, $3$, $2$ and $1$ pins.
Two consecutive triangular numbers add to a square: $T_n+T_{n+1}=(n+1)^2$.
Non-example: The number $8$ is not triangular, because it lies between $T_3=6$ and $T_4=10$.

steps: The $k$-gonal number $P_k(n)=\big((k-2)n^2-(k-4)n\big)/2$ is the $n$-th number for $k$-sided polygons.
Put $k=3$, the case of a triangle.
Then $P_3(n)=n(n+1)/2$, which is the $n$-th triangular number.
links.why: Triangular numbers are the three-sided case of the polygonal numbers.

reminder: In a unique factorization domain, every nonzero non-unit is a product of [irreducible elements](c:irreducible) in exactly one way, up to order and [units](c:group-of-units).
definition: A unique factorization domain (UFD) is an [integral domain](c:integral-domain) in which every nonzero non-unit is a finite product of [irreducible elements](c:irreducible), that is, of non-units that are not products of two non-units. Two such factorizations of the same element have the same number of factors, and after reordering they differ only by multiplication by [units](c:group-of-units).
examples: The integers $\mathbb{Z}$ are a UFD: $12=2\cdot2\cdot3$, up to order and signs.
A polynomial ring $K[x]$ over a field $K$ is a UFD: every polynomial factors uniquely into irreducible polynomials, up to constants.
The ring $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ is a UFD by Gauss's lemma, although it is not a principal ideal domain.
Non-example: In $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$, we have $6=2\cdot3=(1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$, two different factorizations into irreducible elements.

steps: Take a [principal ideal domain](c:principal-ideal-domain) $R$, which is Noetherian.
Noetherian gives a factorization of every nonzero non-unit into irreducible elements.
In a principal ideal domain, every irreducible element is prime.
Prime factors force the factorization to be unique up to order and units, so $R$ is a UFD.
links.why: Every principal ideal domain is a unique factorization domain, but $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ shows that the converse fails.

steps: Take a UFD $R$ and two nonzero elements $a$ and $b$.
Factor both elements into irreducible elements.
For each irreducible element, keep the smaller of its two exponents, and multiply the results.
The product divides $a$ and $b$ and is divisible by every common divisor, so it is a gcd.
links.why: Every UFD has gcds, but a domain with gcds need not have unique factorization.

steps: Start with an [integral domain](c:integral-domain) $R$.
Require that every nonzero non-unit factors into irreducible elements.
Require that this factorization is unique up to order and units.
links.why: A UFD is an integral domain with one extra property, so every fact about integral domains applies.

reminder: The unit ball around a point of a [metric space](c:metric-space) is the set of points at distance at most $1$ from it.
definition: In a [metric space](c:metric-space) $(X,d)$, the unit ball around a point $x\in X$ is the [set](c:set) $\{y\in X : d(x,y)\le1\}$. In a [normed space](c:normed-space), the unit ball around $0$ is $\{y:\|y\|\le1\}$. The open unit ball uses $d(x,y)<1$ instead.
examples: In $\mathbb{R}$ with the usual distance, the unit ball around $0$ is the interval $[-1,1]$.
In $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the Euclidean norm, the unit ball is the closed disc; with the max norm, it is the square $[-1,1]^2$.
In $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the $\ell^1$ norm, the unit ball is the diamond $|x|+|y|\le1$.
Non-example: The unit sphere $\{y:d(x,y)=1\}$ is not the unit ball, because it omits the points closer than $1$ to $x$.

steps: A [ball](c:ball) $B(x,r)=\{y:d(x,y)\le r\}$ has a center $x$ and a radius $r>0$.
Fix the radius $r=1$.
The ball $B(x,1)$ is the unit ball around $x$.
links.why: The unit ball is the ball of radius $1$; in a normed space, scaling by $r$ turns it into any ball.

reminder: A word over a set is a finite sequence of elements of that set, written one after another.
definition: A word over a [set](c:set) $A$, the alphabet, is a finite [sequence](c:sequence) $a_1a_2\cdots a_n$ of elements of $A$; the number $n\ge0$ is its length. The empty word has length $0$. Words are the elements of the free monoid on $A$, where the product of two words is their concatenation.
examples: Over $A=\{a,b\}$, the words include $abba$, $a$ and the empty word.
The word $1011$ over $\{0,1\}$ has length $4$.
In a group generated by $g$ and $h$, the product $gh^{-1}g$ is the value of the word $g\,h^{-1}\,g$.
Non-example: The infinite sequence $a,a,a,\dots$ is not a word, because a word has finite length.

steps: A [sequence](c:sequence) over $A$ assigns an element of $A$ to each index in some index set.
Take the index set $\{1,\dots,n\}$ for some $n\ge0$.
A sequence with an index set of this form is a word of length $n$.
links.why: A word is a finite sequence, so facts about sequences apply to words.

reminder: An abelian variety is a [complete](c:complete-variety) connected [algebraic group](c:algebraic-group); equivalently, a projective variety with a compatible group law.
definition: An abelian variety over a field $k$ is a complete, connected [algebraic group](c:algebraic-group) $A$ over $k$, that is, a [complete](c:complete-variety) [algebraic variety](c:algebraic-variety) whose multiplication and inverse are morphisms. Such a group is automatically commutative and projective.
examples: An [elliptic curve](c:elliptic-curve) is an abelian variety of dimension $1$.
The [Jacobian](c:jacobian-variety) of a smooth projective curve is an abelian variety.
A product $A\times B$ of abelian varieties is an abelian variety.
Non-example: The multiplicative group $\mathbb{G}_m$ is an algebraic group, but it is not complete, so it is not an abelian variety.

steps: Start with an [algebraic group](c:algebraic-group) $G$ over $k$.
Require that $G$ is connected.
Require that $G$ is a complete variety.
Such a group is an abelian variety, and it is automatically commutative.
links.why: An abelian variety is an algebraic group with two extra conditions, connectedness and completeness.

steps: An elliptic curve is a smooth projective curve of genus $1$ with a chosen point.
The chosen point is the identity of a group law given by morphisms.
So the curve is a complete connected algebraic group of dimension $1$, an abelian variety.
links.why: Elliptic curves are the one-dimensional abelian varieties.

steps: Let $C$ be a smooth projective curve.
Its Jacobian is the group of degree-zero line bundles on $C$ up to isomorphism, with an algebraic structure.
This group is complete and connected, so it is an abelian variety whose dimension is the genus of $C$.
links.why: Jacobians are the main source of abelian varieties.

reminder: A [measure](c:measure) $\mu$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\nu$ when every [null set](c:null-set) of $\nu$ is a null set of $\mu$.
definition:
Let $\mu$ and $
u$ be [measures](c:measure) on the same [measurable space](c:measurable-space) $(X,\mathcal{A})$. Then $\mu$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $
u$, written $\mu\ll
u$, if $\mu(A)=0$ for every $A\in\mathcal{A}$ with $
u(A)=0$. If both measures are $\sigma$-finite, this holds exactly when $\mu$ has a density with respect to $
u$.
examples: Every measure $\mu(A)=\int_Af\,d\lambda$ with a density $f\ge0$ is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure $\lambda$.
The standard Gaussian measure on $\mathbb{R}$ is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure.
Every measure is absolutely continuous with respect to itself.
Non-example: The Dirac measure $\delta_0$ is not absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure, because $\delta_0(\{0\})=1$ but $\lambda(\{0\})=0$.

reminder: A sequence of [random variables](c:random-variable) converges almost surely when it converges at every outcome outside an event of probability zero.
definition: Let $(X_n)$ and $X$ be [random variables](c:random-variable) on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)$. Then $X_n\to X$ almost surely if the set of outcomes $\omega$ with $X_n(\omega)\to X(\omega)$ is an event of probability $1$. This is convergence [almost everywhere](c:almost-everywhere) for the measure $P$, with the [limit](c:limit-of-a-sequence) taken at each outcome.
examples: The strong law of large numbers says that the sample means of iid integrable variables converge almost surely to their mean.
If $U$ is uniform on $[0,1]$ and $X_n=U^n$, then $X_n\to0$ almost surely, because $U<1$ with probability $1$.
If $X_n=Z/n$ for a fixed real random variable $Z$, then $X_n\to0$ at every outcome.
Non-example: Let $A_n$ be independent events with $P(A_n)=1/n$. Then $\mathbf{1}_{A_n}\to0$ in probability but not almost surely, because $\sum1/n$ diverges (second Borel-Cantelli lemma).

steps: Take random variables with $X_n(\omega)\to X(\omega)$ at every outcome $\omega$, that is, with [pointwise convergence](c:pointwise-convergence).
The set of outcomes where convergence fails is then empty.
The empty set is an event of probability zero, so $X_n\to X$ almost surely.
links.why: Almost sure convergence relaxes pointwise convergence by allowing a failure set of probability zero.

reminder: A Baire space is a [topological space](c:topological-space) in which every countable intersection of dense open sets is dense.
definition: A [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is a Baire space if the intersection of every countable family of [dense](c:dense-set) [open sets](c:open-set) of $X$ is dense in $X$. Equivalently, every countable union of closed sets with empty interior has empty interior.
examples: Every complete metric space is a Baire space (the Baire category theorem), for example $\mathbb{R}^n$.
Every locally compact Hausdorff space is a Baire space.
The irrational numbers $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ form a Baire space, because they are completely metrizable.
Non-example: The rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$ are not a Baire space, because $\mathbb{Q}$ is the countable union of its single points, which are closed with empty interior.

steps: Let $X$ be a [complete metric space](c:complete-metric-space), let $U_n$ be dense open sets, and let $W$ be a nonempty open set.
Choose nested closed balls of radius below $1/n$, with the $n$-th ball inside $W\cap U_1\cap\cdots\cap U_n$.
Completeness gives a point in all the balls, and this point lies in $W$ and in every $U_n$.
So $\bigcap_nU_n$ meets every nonempty open set, and $X$ is a Baire space.
links.why: This is the Baire category theorem: completeness is a sufficient condition for the Baire property.

steps: Let $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorff space, let $U_n$ be dense open sets, and let $W$ be a nonempty open set.
Choose nonempty open sets $V_n$ with compact closures, with $\overline{V_{n+1}}\subseteq V_n\cap U_{n+1}$ and $\overline{V_1}\subseteq W\cap U_1$.
The nested compact closures have a common point, which lies in $W$ and in every $U_n$.
So $\bigcap_nU_n$ is dense, and $X$ is a Baire space.
links.why: Local compactness is a second sufficient condition for the Baire property, and it covers spaces that are not metrizable.

reminder: A bounded continuous function is a [continuous function](c:continuous-function) whose values all lie within some fixed distance of each other.
definition: A bounded continuous function from a [topological space](c:topological-space) $\alpha$ to a [metric space](c:metric-space) $\beta$ is a [continuous function](c:continuous-function) $f:\alpha\to\beta$ for which there is a constant $C$ with $d(f(x),f(y))\le C$ for all $x,y\in\alpha$. For real-valued $f$, this means $|f|\le M$ for some $M$. Such functions are written $C_b(\alpha,\beta)$.
examples: The function $\sin:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is bounded and continuous.
The function $x\mapsto1/(1+x^2)$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is bounded and continuous.
Every continuous real function on a compact space is bounded and continuous.
Non-example: The function $x\mapsto x$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is continuous but not bounded, and the step function $\mathbf{1}_{[0,\infty)}$ is bounded but not continuous.

steps: Start with a [bounded function](c:bounded-function) $f:\alpha\to\beta$ from a topological space to a metric space.
Add the condition that $f$ is continuous.
The functions with both properties are the bounded continuous functions.
links.why: Bounded continuous functions form a closed subspace of the bounded functions under the supremum distance.

steps: Start with a [continuous function](c:continuous-function) $f:\alpha\to\beta$.
Add the condition that $d(f(x),f(y))\le C$ for some constant $C$ and all $x,y$.
Such an $f$ is a bounded continuous function.
links.why: On a compact space the extra condition is automatic, so every continuous function there is bounded.

reminder: A bounded set in a [metric space](c:metric-space) fits inside some [ball](c:ball) of finite radius.
definition: A [subset](c:subset) $S$ of a [metric space](c:metric-space) $X$ is bounded if some [ball](c:ball) of finite radius contains $S$. Equivalently, $S$ is empty or its [diameter](c:diameter) is finite. In $\mathbb{R}^n$, this means that there is a [real number](c:real-number) $R$ with $|x|\le R$ for all $x\in S$.
examples: Every finite subset of a metric space is bounded.
The interval $[0,1]$ is bounded in $\mathbb{R}$, and the open unit disc is bounded in $\mathbb{R}^2$.
Every compact subset of a metric space is bounded.
Non-example: The set $\mathbb{Z}$ is not bounded in $\mathbb{R}$, because no ball of finite radius contains all integers.

steps: Let $S$ be [totally bounded](c:totally-bounded-space), so finitely many balls of radius $1$ cover $S$.
Let $c_1,\dots,c_k$ be their centers, and let $D$ be the largest of the distances $d(c_1,c_i)$.
Every point of $S$ lies within distance $D+1$ of $c_1$.
So $S$ lies in a ball of radius $D+1$, and $S$ is bounded.
links.why: Every totally bounded set is bounded; the converse holds in $\mathbb{R}^n$ but fails in general.

reminder: A closed manifold is a [compact](c:compact-space) [manifold](c:manifold) without boundary.
definition: A closed manifold is a [manifold](c:manifold) that is [compact](c:compact-space) and has empty [boundary](c:boundary). In contrast, a manifold without boundary whose connected components are all non-compact is an open manifold.
examples: The sphere $S^n$ is a closed manifold.
The torus $T^2$ and the real projective plane $\mathbb{RP}^2$ are closed manifolds.
Every compact Lie group, such as $SO(3)$, is a closed manifold.
Non-example: The closed disc $D^2$ is compact but has the circle as its boundary, and the plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ has no boundary but is not compact.

steps: Start with a [manifold](c:manifold) $M$.
Require that $M$ is compact.
Require that $M$ has no boundary points.
links.why: A closed manifold is a manifold with two extra conditions, which give tools such as finite-dimensional cohomology and Poincaré duality.

steps: The [sphere](c:sphere) $S^n$ is compact, because it is closed and bounded in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$.
Near each point, $S^n$ looks like $\mathbb{R}^n$, and it has no boundary points.
So $S^n$ is a closed manifold.
links.why: Spheres are the simplest closed manifolds, and they give a first test for statements about closed manifolds.

reminder: The commutant of a set $S$ is the set of all elements that commute with every element of $S$.
definition: Let $A$ be an [algebra](c:algebra) and let $S$ be a [subset](c:subset) of $A$. The commutant of $S$ is $S'=\{a\in A:as=sa\text{ for all }s\in S\}$. For a set of [bounded operators](c:bounded-linear-operator) on a Hilbert space, $A$ is the algebra of all bounded operators. The commutant is always a subalgebra of $A$, and $S\subseteq S''$.
examples: The commutant of $\{1\}$ is the whole algebra $A$.
In $M_n(\mathbb{C})$, the commutant of the diagonal matrices is the set of diagonal matrices.
In $M_n(\mathbb{C})$, the commutant of the whole algebra is the set of scalar matrices.
Non-example: The matrix unit $E_{12}$ is not in the commutant of $\{E_{11}\}$, because $E_{11}E_{12}=E_{12}$ but $E_{12}E_{11}=0$.

steps: Take $S=A$, the whole algebra.
The commutant $A'$ is the set of elements that commute with every element of $A$.
That set is the [center](c:center) of $A$.
links.why: The center is the commutant of the whole algebra, so results on commutants also describe centers.

reminder: A complete graph is a [graph](c:graph) in which every two different vertices are joined by an edge.
definition: A complete graph on $n$ vertices, written $K_n$, is a simple undirected [graph](c:graph) in which each pair of distinct [vertices](c:vertex) is joined by exactly one [edge](c:edge). It has $n(n-1)/2$ edges.
examples: The graph $K_3$ is a triangle, and $K_4$ has $6$ edges.
A single vertex $K_1$ and a single edge $K_2$ are complete graphs.
In a group of people where every two people shake hands, the handshake graph is complete.
Non-example: The path with three vertices $a-b-c$ is not complete, because $a$ and $c$ are not joined.

steps: Start with a simple undirected [graph](c:graph) $G=(V,E)$.
Require that every pair of distinct vertices in $V$ is an edge in $E$.
Then $E$ has all $n(n-1)/2$ possible edges, and $G$ is the complete graph $K_n$.
links.why: A complete graph is the graph with the most possible edges, the extreme case in results on edge density.

reminder: The complex derivative of $f$ at $z_0$ is the limit of $(f(z_0+h)-f(z_0))/h$ as the complex number $h$ tends to $0$.
definition: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb{C}$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb{C}$ be a [function](c:function). The complex derivative at $z_0\in U$ is $f'(z_0)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(z_0+h)-f(z_0)}{h}$, if this [limit](c:limit-of-a-function) exists as the [complex number](c:complex-number) $h\ne0$ tends to $0$ in every direction.
examples: For $f(z)=z^2$, the quotient is $2z_0+h$, so $f'(z_0)=2z_0$.
For $f(z)=|z|^2$, the complex derivative exists only at $z_0=0$.
Non-example: The function $f(z)=\bar z$ has no complex derivative at any point, because the quotient is $1$ for real $h$ and $-1$ for imaginary $h$.

steps: Regard $\mathbb{C}$ as the real plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $f$ as a map $\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^2$.
If $f$ has a complex derivative $a=f'(z_0)$, then $f(z_0+h)=f(z_0)+ah+o(|h|)$.
So the real [derivative](c:derivative) of $f$ at $z_0$ is the real-linear map $h\mapsto ah$, multiplication by $a$.
Thus complex differentiability is real differentiability with a derivative of the special form $h\mapsto ah$.
links.why: It shows what is special in the complex case: the real derivative is multiplication by one complex number, which gives the Cauchy-Riemann equations.

reminder: A critical point of a smooth map is a point where the derivative has rank less than the dimension of the target.
definition: Let $f:X\to Y$ be a [smooth function](c:smooth-function) between smooth manifolds. A point $x\in X$ is critical if the [derivative](c:derivative) $df_x:T_xX\to T_{f(x)}Y$ has [rank](c:rank) less than $\dim Y$, that is, if $df_x$ is not surjective. For a real-valued $f$, this means $df_x=0$.
examples: For $f(x)=x^3$ on $\mathbb{R}$, the point $0$ is critical, because $f'(0)=0$.
For $f(x,y)=x^2-y^2$, the origin is a critical point, a saddle.
Every point is critical for a constant map to $\mathbb{R}$.
Non-example: For $f(x)=x$, the derivative is $1$ at every point, so $f$ has no critical point.

reminder: A diagonal matrix is a [square matrix](c:square-matrix) whose entries off the diagonal are all zero.
definition: A [square matrix](c:square-matrix) $A=(a_{ij})$ is diagonal if $a_{ij}=0$ whenever $i\ne j$. Its only possibly nonzero entries $a_{11},\dots,a_{nn}$ lie on the main diagonal, and one writes $A=\operatorname{diag}(a_{11},\dots,a_{nn})$.
examples: The identity matrix $I_n$ and the zero matrix are diagonal.
The matrix $\operatorname{diag}(2,-1,5)$ has the entries $2$, $-1$ and $5$ on its diagonal.
Diagonal matrices multiply entry by entry: $\operatorname{diag}(a_i)\operatorname{diag}(b_i)=\operatorname{diag}(a_ib_i)$.
Non-example: The matrix with rows $(1,1)$ and $(0,1)$ is not diagonal, because its entry in row $1$, column $2$ is not zero.

steps: Take a diagonal matrix $A$; its entries below the diagonal are $0$.
A matrix whose entries below the diagonal are all $0$ is upper triangular.
Its entries above the diagonal are also $0$, so $A$ is lower triangular as well.
links.why: The diagonal matrices are exactly the matrices that are both upper and lower triangular.

steps: The [identity matrix](c:identity-matrix) $I_n$ has $1$ in each diagonal position.
All its off-diagonal entries are $0$.
So $I_n$ is the diagonal matrix $\operatorname{diag}(1,\dots,1)$.
links.why: The identity matrix is the diagonal matrix with all diagonal entries equal to $1$.

reminder: The diameter of a subset of a [metric space](c:metric-space) is the supremum of the distances between its points.
definition: Let $S$ be a [subset](c:subset) of a [metric space](c:metric-space) $(X,d)$. The diameter of $S$ is $\operatorname{diam}S=\sup\{d(x,y):x,y\in S\}$, the [least upper bound](c:least-upper-bound) of the distances between points of $S$. By convention it is $0$ for the empty set, and it is $\infty$ when the distances are unbounded.
examples: The interval $[a,b]$ in $\mathbb{R}$ has diameter $b-a$.
The open unit disc in $\mathbb{R}^2$ has diameter $2$, although no two of its points have distance $2$.
Non-example: The set $\mathbb{Z}\subset\mathbb{R}$ has no finite diameter, because the distances between integers are unbounded.

reminder: A differential $k$-form gives each point of a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) an alternating $k$-linear function on tangent vectors, varying smoothly.
definition: A differential $k$-form on a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$ is a smooth section of the $k$-th [exterior power](c:exterior-algebra) $\Lambda^kT^*M$ of the [cotangent bundle](c:cotangent-bundle). In local coordinates, it is a sum $\sum f_{i_1\dots i_k}\,dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_k}$ with smooth coefficient functions. A $k$-form can be integrated over an oriented $k$-dimensional submanifold.
examples: A smooth function is a $0$-form, and the differential $df$ of a smooth function $f$ is a $1$-form.
On $\mathbb{R}^2$, the expression $dx\wedge dy$ is a $2$-form, the area form.
On the circle, $d\theta$ is a $1$-form whose integral over the circle is $2\pi$.
Non-example: The vector field $\partial/\partial x$ is a section of the tangent bundle, not of an exterior power of the cotangent bundle, so it is not a differential form.

steps: Take a [closed differential form](c:closed-differential-form) $\omega$, one with $d\omega=0$.
Forget the condition $d\omega=0$.
What remains is a smooth section of $\Lambda^kT^*M$, which is a differential form.
links.why: Closed forms are the differential forms with $d\omega=0$, and they define de Rham cohomology classes.

reminder: The discriminant of a [polynomial](c:polynomial) is zero exactly when the polynomial has a repeated root.
definition: For a [polynomial](c:polynomial) $p(x)=a_n\prod_{i=1}^{n}(x-r_i)$ of degree $n$ with [roots](c:root-of-a-polynomial) $r_1,\dots,r_n$, the discriminant is $\operatorname{disc}(p)=a_n^{2n-2}\prod_{i<j}(r_i-r_j)^2$. It is a polynomial in the coefficients of $p$, and it is zero exactly when two roots coincide. For $ax^2+bx+c$, it is $b^2-4ac$.
examples: The polynomial $ax^2+bx+c$ has discriminant $b^2-4ac$, so $x^2-2x+1$ has discriminant $0$.
The polynomial $x^3+px+q$ has discriminant $-4p^3-27q^2$.
The polynomial $x^2-1$ has discriminant $4$, and its roots $1$ and $-1$ are distinct.
Non-example: The product $\prod_{i<j}(r_i-r_j)$ without the square is not the discriminant, because it changes sign when two roots swap.

reminder: A family of functions is equicontinuous when, for each point and $\varepsilon$, one $\delta$ works for every function in the family.
definition: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a family of [functions](c:function) from a [metric space](c:metric-space) $X$ to a metric space $Y$. The family $\mathcal{F}$ is equicontinuous if for every $x\in X$ and every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a $\delta>0$ with $d_Y(f(x),f(y))<\varepsilon$ for all $f\in\mathcal{F}$ and all $y$ with $d_X(x,y)<\delta$. The number $\delta$ depends on $x$ and $\varepsilon$, but not on $f$.
examples: A finite family of [continuous functions](c:continuous-function) on a metric space is equicontinuous.
The family of all $K$-Lipschitz functions $X\to Y$, for fixed $K>0$, is equicontinuous: take $\delta=\varepsilon/K$.
The family $\{x\mapsto\sin(x+a):a\in\mathbb{R}\}$ is equicontinuous, because each member is $1$-Lipschitz.
Non-example: The family $\{x^n:n\ge1\}$ on $[0,1]$ is not equicontinuous at $x=1$, because for $\varepsilon=1/2$ no single $\delta$ works for all $n$.

steps: Take a family $\mathcal{F}=\{f\}$ with one function.
The condition says that for each $x$ and $\varepsilon$, some $\delta$ gives $d(f(x),f(y))<\varepsilon$ when $d(x,y)<\delta$.
This is exactly the continuity of $f$ at every point.
links.why: Equicontinuity asks for one common $\delta$ across a whole family; for one function it is ordinary continuity.

reminder: A path $q(t)$ that makes the action $\int L\,dt$ stationary satisfies $\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial q}$.
definition: Let $L(t,q,\dot q)$ be a smooth Lagrangian, and let $S[q]=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}L(t,q(t),\dot q(t))\,dt$ be the action. The Euler-Lagrange equation uses [partial derivatives](c:partial-derivative) of $L$ and the [derivative](c:derivative) in $t$: $\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q}-\frac{\partial L}{\partial q}=0$. A smooth path $q$ with fixed end points makes $S$ stationary exactly when it solves this equation.
examples: For $L=\tfrac12m\dot q^2-V(q)$, the equation is $m\ddot q=-V'(q)$, which is Newton's law.
For the arc-length Lagrangian $L=\sqrt{1+\dot q^2}$, the equation gives $\ddot q=0$, so the extremal curves are straight lines.
Non-example: For $L=\tfrac12\dot q^2$, the path $q(t)=t^2$ does not satisfy the equation, because $\ddot q=2\ne0$, so it is not stationary for fixed end points.

reminder: The expectation value of a [random variable](c:random-variable) is its average value under the given probabilities.
definition: Let $X$ be an integrable [random variable](c:random-variable) on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)$, with [probability measure](c:probability-measure) $P$. Its expectation value is $E[X]=\int_\Omega X\,dP$, a [Lebesgue integral](c:lebesgue-integral). For a variable with finitely many values, this is $\sum_xx\,P(X=x)$.
examples: A fair die has expectation value $(1+2+3+4+5+6)/6=3.5$.
A Bernoulli variable with success probability $p$ has expectation value $p$.
For an event $A$, the indicator variable has $E[\mathbf{1}_A]=P(A)$.
Non-example: A Cauchy distributed variable has no expectation value, because the integral $\int|x|/(\pi(1+x^2))\,dx$ diverges.

steps: Take a random variable $X$ and an integer $k\ge1$.
The function $X^k$ is again a random variable.
Its expectation value $E[X^k]$ is the $k$-th [moment](c:moment) of $X$.
links.why: Moments are expectation values of powers, so facts about expectation values apply to every moment.

steps: Take the trivial $\sigma$-algebra $\{\emptyset,\Omega\}$, which carries no information.
A function that is measurable for this $\sigma$-algebra is constant.
The [conditional expectation](c:conditional-expectation) of $X$ given this $\sigma$-algebra is the constant $E[X]$.
links.why: The expectation value is the conditional expectation given no information.

reminder: An extreme point of a [convex set](c:convex-set) is a point that is not strictly between two different points of the set.
definition: Let $C$ be a [convex set](c:convex-set) in a real [vector space](c:vector-space). A point $x\in C$ is an extreme point if $x=ty+(1-t)z$ with $y,z\in C$ and $0<t<1$ implies $y=z=x$. Equivalently, the set $C\setminus\{x\}$ is still convex.
examples: The four corners of a square are its extreme points.
Every point of the unit circle is an extreme point of the closed unit disc.
The extreme points of a closed segment $[a,b]$ are $a$ and $b$.
Non-example: The midpoint of a side of a square is not an extreme point, because it lies between the two corners of that side.

reminder: The field of fractions of an [integral domain](c:integral-domain) is the smallest [field](c:field) that contains it, made of fractions $a/b$ with $b\ne0$.
definition: Let $D$ be an [integral domain](c:integral-domain). Its field of fractions $\operatorname{Frac}(D)$ is the set of classes $a/b$ with $a,b\in D$ and $b\ne0$, where $a/b=c/d$ exactly when $ad=bc$, with the usual addition and multiplication of fractions. The map $a\mapsto a/1$ embeds $D$ in the [field](c:field) $\operatorname{Frac}(D)$, and every injective ring map from $D$ into a field extends uniquely to it. It is the [localization](c:localization-of-a-ring) of $D$ at the nonzero elements.
examples: The field of fractions of $\mathbb{Z}$ is $\mathbb{Q}$.
The field of fractions of $K[x]$ is the field $K(x)$ of rational functions.
The field of fractions of $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ is $\mathbb{Q}(i)$.
Non-example: The ring $\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}$ has no field of fractions, because $2\cdot3=0$ with $2,3\ne0$, so it is not an integral domain.

steps: Take an integral domain $D$ and the set $S=D\setminus\{0\}$ of nonzero elements.
The set $S$ is multiplicative, because a domain has no zero divisors.
Invert all elements of $S$ to form the [localization](c:localization-of-a-ring) $S^{-1}D$.
Every nonzero fraction $a/b$ has the inverse $b/a$, so $S^{-1}D$ is a field.
links.why: The field of fractions is the localization in which every nonzero element becomes invertible.

reminder: A flat connection is a [connection](c:connection-on-a-bundle) on a bundle whose [curvature](c:curvature) is zero everywhere.
definition: Let $\nabla$ be a [connection on a bundle](c:connection-on-a-bundle) $E\to M$. It is flat if its [curvature](c:curvature) $F_\nabla$ vanishes at every point. For a vector bundle, this holds exactly when every point has a neighbourhood with a frame of parallel sections.
examples: The trivial connection $d$ on a trivial vector bundle is flat.
The Levi-Civita connection of the flat torus $\mathbb{R}^2/\mathbb{Z}^2$ is flat.
Every connection on a bundle over a circle is flat, because the curvature is a $2$-form and the circle has dimension $1$.
Non-example: The Levi-Civita connection of the round sphere $S^2$ has curvature that is not zero, so it is not flat.

steps: Start with a [connection](c:connection-on-a-bundle) $\nabla$ on a bundle $E\to M$.
Compute its curvature $F_\nabla$.
Require that its curvature is zero, that is, $F_\nabla=0$ everywhere.
A connection with this property is flat.
links.why: Flat connections have parallel transport that depends only on the homotopy class of a path.

reminder: A generating function packs a [sequence](c:sequence) $a_n$ into the [formal power series](c:formal-power-series) $\sum a_nx^n$.
definition: The (ordinary) generating function of a [sequence](c:sequence) $(a_n)_{n\ge0}$ is the [formal power series](c:formal-power-series) $A(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n$. The coefficient of $x^n$ is $a_n$, so operations on series, such as sums and products, express facts about the sequence. Variants use other weights, for example $\sum a_nx^n/n!$ for the exponential generating function.
examples: The sequence $1,1,1,\dots$ has the generating function $1/(1-x)$.
The binomial coefficients $\binom{n}{k}$ for fixed $n$ have the generating function $(1+x)^n$.
The Fibonacci numbers have the generating function $x/(1-x-x^2)$.
Non-example: The sum $\sum a_n$ has no variable $x$ and loses the position $n$ of each term, so it does not encode the sequence.

reminder: A [graph](c:graph) $H$ is a minor of a graph $G$ when $H$ comes from $G$ by deleting vertices, deleting edges and contracting edges.
definition: A [graph](c:graph) $H$ is a minor of a graph $G$ if some sequence of operations on $G$ gives a graph isomorphic to $H$. The operations are: delete a [vertex](c:vertex), delete an [edge](c:edge), and contract an edge, which merges its two ends into one vertex.
examples: The triangle $K_3$ is a minor of every cycle $C_n$ with $n\ge3$: contract edges until three are left.
Contracting a perfect matching of the Petersen graph gives $K_5$, so $K_5$ is a minor of it.
Every subgraph of $G$ is a minor of $G$, because deletions alone give it.
Non-example: The graph $K_4$ is not a minor of a tree, because deleting and contracting keeps a forest, and $K_4$ has cycles.

steps: Let $H$ be a [subgraph](c:is-subgraph) of $G$.
Delete the vertices and edges of $G$ that are not in $H$.
No contraction is needed, so $H$ is a minor of $G$.
links.why: Minors allow contractions in addition to deletions, so the minor relation is weaker than the subgraph relation.

reminder: A Hamiltonian cycle in a graph is a cycle that passes through every vertex exactly once.
definition: A Hamiltonian cycle of a [graph](c:graph) $G$ is a [cycle](c:cycle) in $G$ that contains every [vertex](c:vertex) of $G$. In other words, it is a closed [path](c:path) that passes through every vertex exactly once and returns to its start.
examples: A cycle graph $C_n$ is its own Hamiltonian cycle.
The cube graph $Q_3$ has a Hamiltonian cycle given by a Gray code on $3$ bits.
Every complete graph $K_n$ with $n\ge3$ has a Hamiltonian cycle.
Non-example: The Petersen graph has no Hamiltonian cycle, and a path graph has no cycle at all.

steps: Take a [cycle](c:cycle) $C$ in the graph $G$, a closed path whose only repeated vertex is its start.
Require that $C$ passes through every vertex of $G$.
A cycle with this property is a Hamiltonian cycle.
links.why: A Hamiltonian cycle is a spanning cycle, so facts about cycles apply to it.

reminder: A highest weight vector is a weight vector that every positive root vector sends to zero, and its weight is the highest weight.
definition: Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a semisimple [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) with a [Cartan subalgebra](c:cartan-subalgebra) $\mathfrak{h}$ and a choice of positive roots of its [root system](c:is-root-system), and let $V$ be a [representation](c:lie-algebra-representation) of $\mathfrak{g}$. A highest weight vector is a nonzero [eigenvector](c:eigenvector) $v\in V$ of $\mathfrak{h}$ with $e_\alpha v=0$ for every positive root vector $e_\alpha$, and its weight $\lambda\in\mathfrak{h}^*$ is the highest weight. Each finite-dimensional irreducible representation has a unique highest weight, which determines it up to isomorphism.
examples: For $\mathfrak{sl}_2$, the irreducible representation of dimension $n+1$ has highest weight $n$, with highest weight vector $x^n$ in the polynomials of degree $n$ in $x$ and $y$.
The trivial representation has highest weight $0$.
In the adjoint representation of $\mathfrak{sl}_n$, the highest weight is the highest root, with highest weight vector $E_{1n}$.

Non-example: In the $3$-dimensional representation of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$, the vector of weight $0$ is not a highest weight vector, because $e$ sends it to a nonzero multiple of the vector of weight $2$.

steps: Take a vector $v\in V$ that is an [eigenvector](c:eigenvector) of all of $\mathfrak{h}$ at once; its eigenvalue is a weight.
Add the condition that $e_\alpha v=0$ for every positive root vector $e_\alpha$.
A weight vector with this extra property is a highest weight vector.
links.why: A highest weight vector is a simultaneous eigenvector of the Cartan subalgebra that positive root vectors kill.

reminder: A Hopf algebra is a [bialgebra](c:bialgebra) with an antipode, a map that acts like the inverse of a group.
definition: A Hopf algebra over a field $K$ is a [bialgebra](c:bialgebra) $(H,m,\eta,\Delta,\varepsilon)$ with a linear map $S:H\to H$, the antipode, such that $m\circ(S\otimes\mathrm{id})\circ\Delta=\eta\circ\varepsilon=m\circ(\mathrm{id}\otimes S)\circ\Delta$. A bialgebra is an [algebra](c:algebra-over-a-field) and a [coalgebra](c:coalgebra) with compatible structure maps, and the antipode generalizes the map $g\mapsto g^{-1}$ of a group.
examples: The group algebra $K[G]$, with $\Delta(g)=g\otimes g$, $\varepsilon(g)=1$ and $S(g)=g^{-1}$, is a Hopf algebra.
The polynomial algebra $K[x]$, with $\Delta(x)=x\otimes1+1\otimes x$ and $S(x)=-x$, is a Hopf algebra.
The algebra of functions on a finite group is a Hopf algebra, with $S(f)(g)=f(g^{-1})$.
Non-example: The monoid algebra $K[\mathbb{N}]$ with $\Delta(x)=x\otimes x$ is a bialgebra with no antipode, because $x$ has no inverse.

steps: Start with a [bialgebra](c:bialgebra) $H$ with product $m$ and coproduct $\Delta$.
Look for a linear map $S:H\to H$ with $m(S\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta=\eta\varepsilon=m(\mathrm{id}\otimes S)\Delta$.
If such a map exists, it is unique, and $H$ is a Hopf algebra.
links.why: A Hopf algebra is a bialgebra with one extra piece of structure, the antipode, which is unique when it exists.

steps: Take a group $G$ and its [group algebra](c:group-algebra) $K[G]$.
Define $\Delta(g)=g\otimes g$ and $\varepsilon(g)=1$ on group elements, and extend linearly.
The map $S(g)=g^{-1}$ is an antipode, so $K[G]$ is a Hopf algebra.
links.why: Group algebras are the basic Hopf algebras, and the antipode of a Hopf algebra is modeled on the inverse of a group.

reminder: An injective map is a [function](c:function) that never sends two different inputs to the same output.
definition: A [function](c:function) $f:A\to B$ is injective if $f(a)=f(a')$ implies $a=a'$ for all $a,a'\in A$. Equivalently, every $b\in B$ has at most one preimage.
examples: The inclusion of a subset $S\subseteq A$ into $A$ is injective.
The map $x\mapsto2x$ from $\mathbb{Z}$ to $\mathbb{Z}$ is injective.
The exponential map $\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is injective.
Non-example: The map $x\mapsto x^2$ from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{R}$ is not injective, because $f(1)=f(-1)$.

steps: Start with any [function](c:function) $f:A\to B$.
Add the condition that $f(a)=f(a')$ forces $a=a'$.
links.why: An injective map is a function with one extra condition, so every fact about functions applies to it.

steps: A [bijection](c:bijection) $f:A\to B$ has a two-sided inverse $g:B\to A$.
If $f(a)=f(a')$, then applying $g$ gives $a=g(f(a))=g(f(a'))=a'$.
So $f$ is injective, and a bijection is an injective map that is also surjective.
links.why: Bijections are exactly the injective maps that are also surjective.

reminder: The interior of a subset $A$ of a [topological space](c:topological-space) is the largest open set contained in $A$.
definition: Let $A$ be a [subset](c:subset) of a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$. The interior $\operatorname{int}A$ is the union of all [open sets](c:open-set) of $X$ that lie inside $A$, so it is the largest open set contained in $A$. A point $x$ lies in $\operatorname{int}A$ exactly when some open neighbourhood of $x$ lies in $A$.
examples: The interior of $[0,1]$ in $\mathbb{R}$ is $(0,1)$.
The interior of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$ is empty.
The interior of an open set is the set itself.
Non-example: The endpoint $0$ is not in the interior of $[0,1]$, because every open set around $0$ contains negative numbers.

reminder: A semisimple Lie algebra is a [direct sum](c:direct-sum) of [simple Lie algebras](c:is-simple).
definition: A finite-dimensional [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak{g}$ over a field of characteristic $0$ is semisimple if it is a [direct sum](c:direct-sum) $\mathfrak{g}_1\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathfrak{g}_k$ of [simple Lie algebras](c:is-simple), each with no ideals except $0$ and itself and with $[\mathfrak{g}_i,\mathfrak{g}_i]\ne0$. Equivalently, $\mathfrak{g}$ has no nonzero solvable ideal, or its Killing form is nondegenerate.
examples: The Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb{C})$ of matrices with trace $0$ is semisimple, and it is even simple.
The Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}_4\cong\mathfrak{sl}_2\oplus\mathfrak{sl}_2$ is semisimple but not simple.

Non-example: The abelian Lie algebra $\mathbb{C}$ is not semisimple, because it is a nonzero solvable ideal of itself; the algebra $\mathfrak{gl}_n$ is not semisimple either, because its center is not zero.

steps: A [simple Lie algebra](c:is-simple) $\mathfrak{g}$ has no ideals except $0$ and $\mathfrak{g}$, and it is not abelian.
Take the direct sum with a single summand, so $\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{g}_1$.
A direct sum of one simple Lie algebra is semisimple.
links.why: Simple Lie algebras are the building blocks, and every semisimple Lie algebra is a direct sum of them.

steps: A [reductive Lie algebra](c:reductive-lie-algebra) is a direct sum of a semisimple Lie algebra and an abelian Lie algebra.
Take the abelian summand to be $0$.
The result is the semisimple Lie algebra itself, so it is reductive.
links.why: A semisimple Lie algebra is a reductive Lie algebra with zero center, so results on reductive algebras apply.

reminder: An isomorphism is a structure-preserving map that has a structure-preserving inverse.
definition: In a [category](c:category), a morphism $f:A\to B$ is an isomorphism if there is a morphism $g:B\to A$ with $g\circ f=\mathrm{id}_A$ and $f\circ g=\mathrm{id}_B$. For groups, rings and modules, it is a [homomorphism](c:homomorphism) that is also a [bijection](c:bijection), and its inverse is then a homomorphism too.
examples: The map $\exp:(\mathbb{R},+)\to(\mathbb{R}_{>0},\cdot)$ is an isomorphism of groups, with inverse $\ln$.
Every real vector space of dimension $n$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^n$ by choosing a basis.
The Chinese remainder theorem gives $\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}\cong\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$.
Non-example: The map $[0,2\pi)\to S^1$, $t\mapsto e^{it}$, is a continuous bijection but not an isomorphism of topological spaces, because its inverse is not continuous.

steps: A [homomorphism](c:homomorphism) $f:A\to B$ preserves the structure.
Require a homomorphism $g:B\to A$ with $g\circ f=\mathrm{id}_A$ and $f\circ g=\mathrm{id}_B$.
A homomorphism with such an inverse is an isomorphism.
links.why: An isomorphism is a homomorphism that can be undone, so isomorphic objects have the same structural properties.

steps: In the category of topological spaces, the morphisms are continuous maps.
An isomorphism there is a continuous map with a continuous inverse.
That is exactly a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism).
links.why: Each kind of structure has its own name for isomorphism; for topological spaces it is homeomorphism.

steps: Take an [automorphism](c:automorphism) of an object $A$, an invertible structure-preserving map $f:A\to A$.
Its inverse $g$ is also structure preserving, and $g\circ f=\mathrm{id}_A=f\circ g$.
So $f$ is an isomorphism from $A$ to $A$.
links.why: Automorphisms are the isomorphisms from an object to itself, and they form the symmetry group of the object.

reminder: A Laurent series is a series $\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}a_n(z-c)^n$ that may contain negative powers of $z-c$.
definition: A Laurent series about $c\in\mathbb{C}$ is a series $\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}a_n(z-c)^n$ with complex coefficients $a_n$; it is the sum of a [power series](c:power-series) in $z-c$ and a power series in $1/(z-c)$. A [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function) on an [annulus](c:annulus) $r<|z-c|<R$ equals its Laurent series there, with unique coefficients.
examples: The function $e^{1/z}=\sum_{n\ge0}z^{-n}/n!$ is a Laurent series about $0$ with infinitely many negative powers.
For $0<|z|<1$, we have $\frac{1}{z(1-z)}=z^{-1}+1+z+z^2+\cdots$.
Every power series is a Laurent series with $a_n=0$ for $n<0$.
Non-example: The expression $\sum_{n\ge0}z^{n/2}$ has fractional powers, so it is not a Laurent series; it is a Puiseux series.

steps: Take a [power series](c:power-series) $\sum_{n\ge0}a_n(z-c)^n$.
Set $a_n=0$ for every $n<0$.
The result is a Laurent series with no negative powers.
links.why: Laurent series extend power series by allowing negative powers, which describe the behavior near a pole.

steps: A [Laurent polynomial](c:laurent-polynomial) is a finite sum $\sum_{n=-m}^{m}a_nz^n$.
It is a Laurent series about $c=0$ with $a_n=0$ for $|n|>m$.
links.why: A Laurent polynomial is a Laurent series with finitely many terms.

reminder: A function is Lipschitz continuous when the distance between values is at most a fixed multiple $K$ of the distance between inputs.
definition: A [function](c:function) $f:X\to Y$ between [metric spaces](c:metric-space) is Lipschitz continuous if there is a constant $K\ge0$ with $d_Y(f(x),f(y))\le K\,d_X(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in X$. The least such $K$ is the Lipschitz constant of $f$.
examples: The absolute value $x\mapsto|x|$ is Lipschitz with $K=1$.
Every linear map between finite-dimensional normed spaces is Lipschitz.
The function $\sin$ is Lipschitz with $K=1$, because $|\cos|\le1$.
Non-example: The function $x\mapsto\sqrt{x}$ on $[0,1]$ is not Lipschitz, because $\sqrt{x}/x=1/\sqrt{x}$ is unbounded near $0$.

steps: Let $f$ be Lipschitz with constant $K>0$, and let $\varepsilon>0$.
Choose the number $\delta=\varepsilon/K$ for this $\varepsilon$.
If $d(x,y)<\delta$, then $d(f(x),f(y))\le K\,d(x,y)<\varepsilon$.
The number $\delta$ does not depend on $x$, so $f$ is [uniformly continuous](c:uniformly-continuous-map).
links.why: Lipschitz continuity is a quantitative form of uniform continuity, with a linear bound.

steps: A [contraction](c:contraction-mapping) $f$ on a metric space has a constant $K<1$ with $d(f(x),f(y))\le K\,d(x,y)$.
This inequality is the Lipschitz condition with the constant $K$.
So every contraction is Lipschitz, and the contraction adds the bound $K<1$.
links.why: Contractions are the Lipschitz maps with constant below $1$, which is the case that has fixed points.

reminder: A matching is a set of edges of a graph in which no two edges share a vertex.
definition: A matching in a [graph](c:graph) $G$ is a set $M$ of [edges](c:edge) of $G$ such that no [vertex](c:vertex) of $G$ is an end of two different edges of $M$. A vertex that is an end of an edge of $M$ is matched by $M$.
examples: A single edge is a matching, and so is the empty set.
In the path $1-2-3-4$, the edges $12$ and $34$ form a matching.
In $K_4$, the edges $12$ and $34$ form a matching that covers every vertex.
Non-example: In the path $1-2-3-4$, the edges $12$ and $23$ do not form a matching, because they share the vertex $2$.

steps: Let $M$ be a [perfect matching](c:perfect-matching) of $G$.
No two edges of $M$ share a vertex.
So $M$ is a matching; the perfect matching adds the condition that every vertex is matched.
links.why: A perfect matching is a matching that covers all vertices, so every result on matchings applies to it.

reminder: A model of a theory is a structure in which every axiom of the theory is true.
definition: Let $T$ be a [theory](c:theory) in a [signature](c:signature-in-logic) $\Sigma$ of function, relation and constant symbols. A model of $T$ is a [structure](c:structure-in-model-theory) $M$ for $\Sigma$, with a set and an interpretation of each symbol, in which every axiom of $T$ is true. In categorical logic, the underlying set can be replaced by an object of another category, such as a topos.
examples: The integers with $+$, $0$ and negation are a model of the theory of groups.
The real numbers with their usual order are a model of the theory of ordered fields.
The rational numbers are a model of the theory of dense linear orders without end points.
Non-example: The structure $(\mathbb{N},+,0)$ is not a model of group theory, because no element $y$ gives $1+y=0$.

steps: Start with a [structure](c:structure-in-model-theory) $M$ for a signature $\Sigma$, that is, a set with interpretations of the symbols.
Fix a theory $T$ whose axioms are sentences in $\Sigma$.
Require that every axiom of $T$ is true in $M$.
Then $M$ is a model of $T$.
links.why: A model is a structure that also satisfies the axioms; every structure is a model of the empty theory.

reminder: An element $x$ of a ring is nilpotent when some positive power of $x$ equals zero.
definition: An element $x$ of a [ring](c:ring) $R$ is nilpotent if there is a [natural number](c:natural-number) $n\ge1$ with $x^n=0$. The zero element is nilpotent, and in a nonzero ring the element $1$ is not nilpotent.
examples: The matrix with rows $(0,1)$ and $(0,0)$ is nilpotent in $M_2(\mathbb{R})$, because its square is $0$.
The class of $2$ in $\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}$ is nilpotent, because $2^2=4=0$.
In $K[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)$, the element $\varepsilon$ is nilpotent.
Non-example: The matrix $\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ satisfies $e^2=e\ne0$, so no power of it is $0$.

reminder: A bilinear form is nondegenerate when the only vector that pairs to zero with every vector is the zero vector.
definition: A [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form) $B:V\times V\to K$ on a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ is nondegenerate if $B(v,w)=0$ for all $w\in V$ implies $v=0$, and $B(w,v)=0$ for all $w\in V$ implies $v=0$. For finite-dimensional $V$, this holds exactly when the matrix of $B$ in a basis is invertible.
examples: The dot product on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is nondegenerate.
The symplectic form $B(x,y)=x_1y_2-x_2y_1$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is nondegenerate.
The form $x_1y_1-x_2y_2-x_3y_3-x_4y_4$ on $\mathbb{R}^4$ is nondegenerate, although it is not positive definite.
Non-example: The form $B(x,y)=x_1y_1$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is degenerate, because $B(e_2,w)=0$ for every $w$.

steps: Start with a [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form) $B$ on $V$.
Check whether some nonzero $v$ has $B(v,w)=0$ for all $w$, or $B(w,v)=0$ for all $w$.
If no such $v$ exists, then $B$ is nondegenerate.
links.why: A nondegenerate form identifies the space with its dual, which a general bilinear form does not do.

steps: Let $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ be an inner product on $V$, and suppose that $\langle v,w\rangle=0$ for all $w$.
Take $w=v$ to get $\langle v,v\rangle=0$.
Positive definiteness gives $v=0$, so the inner product is a nondegenerate form.
links.why: Inner products are the positive definite symmetric forms, and positive definiteness is stronger than nondegeneracy.

reminder: The normal bundle of $X$ in $Y$ is the [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) with fibre $T_yY/T_yX$ at each point $y$ of $X$.
definition: Let $i:X\to Y$ be an [immersion](c:immersion) of smooth manifolds, for example an embedding. The normal bundle $N_i$ is the quotient [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) $i^*TY/TX$ over $X$, where $TX\to i^*TY$ is the injective map of [tangent bundles](c:tangent-bundle) given by the derivative $di$. Its rank is $\dim Y-\dim X$.
examples: The normal bundle of the circle $S^1\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ is a trivial line bundle, spanned by the radial direction.
The normal bundle of the zero section $X\subset E$ of a vector bundle $E$ is $E$ itself.
The normal bundle of the core circle of the Möbius strip is the Möbius line bundle, which is not trivial.
Non-example: The map $t\mapsto(t^2,t^3)$ from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{R}^2$ is not an immersion at $t=0$, because its derivative is $0$ there, so it has no normal bundle in this sense.

reminder: A problem is NP-complete when it lies in [NP](c:np-complexity-class) and every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time.
definition: A decision problem $L$ is NP-complete if $L$ is in [NP](c:np-complexity-class) and every problem $L'$ in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to $L$. Such a reduction is a [function](c:function) $f$, computable in polynomial time, with $x\in L'$ exactly when $f(x)\in L$. If one NP-complete problem can be solved in polynomial time, then every problem in NP can.
examples: The [Boolean satisfiability problem](c:boolean-satisfiability-problem) is NP-complete, by the Cook-Levin theorem.
Deciding whether a graph has a [Hamiltonian cycle](c:hamiltonian-cycle) is NP-complete.
Deciding whether a graph has a proper [coloring](c:graph-coloring) with $3$ colors is NP-complete.
Non-example: The halting problem is NP-hard but not in NP, so it is not NP-complete.

reminder: A null set in a [measure space](c:measure-space) is a measurable set of measure zero, so it can be ignored.
definition: In a [measure space](c:measure-space) $(X,\mathcal{A},\mu)$, a null set is a [measurable set](c:measurable-set) $N\in\mathcal{A}$ with $\mu(N)=0$. Some authors also call every [subset](c:subset) of such a set null. A property that holds outside a null set holds almost everywhere.
examples: Every countable set of real numbers is null for [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure).
The Cantor set is null for Lebesgue measure, although it is uncountable.
The empty set is null for every measure.
Non-example: The interval $[0,1]$ has Lebesgue measure $1$, so it is not null, and the set $\{0\}$ is not null for the Dirac measure $\delta_0$.

steps: Take a [measurable set](c:measurable-set) $N$ in a measure space $(X,\mathcal{A},\mu)$.
Add the condition $\mu(N)=0$.
A measurable set with this property is a null set.
links.why: A null set is a measurable set with measure zero, and countable unions of null sets are again null.

reminder: A parallelogram is a [quadrilateral](c:quadrilateral) whose two pairs of opposite sides are parallel.
definition: A parallelogram is a [quadrilateral](c:quadrilateral) $ABCD$ in the plane with $AB\parallel DC$ and $AD\parallel BC$, that is, both pairs of opposite sides lie on [parallel lines](c:parallel-lines). Its opposite sides have equal length, its opposite angles are equal, and its diagonals bisect each other.
examples: Every [rectangle](c:rectangle) is a parallelogram, and so is every rhombus.
The quadrilateral with vertices $(0,0)$, $(2,0)$, $(3,1)$ and $(1,1)$ is a parallelogram.
Joining the midpoints of the sides of any quadrilateral gives a parallelogram, by Varignon's theorem.
Non-example: A trapezoid with exactly one pair of parallel sides is not a parallelogram.

steps: Start with a [quadrilateral](c:quadrilateral) $ABCD$.
Require that $AB\parallel DC$.
Require that $AD\parallel BC$.
A quadrilateral with both properties is a parallelogram.
links.why: A parallelogram is a quadrilateral with two parallel conditions, and these give equal opposite sides and angles.

steps: Let $ABCD$ be a [rectangle](c:rectangle), so all four angles are right angles.
Sides $AB$ and $DC$ are both perpendicular to $BC$, so they are parallel; likewise $AD$ and $BC$ are both perpendicular to $AB$.
Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, so $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.
links.why: A rectangle is a parallelogram with a right angle, so every fact about parallelograms holds for rectangles.

reminder: An outcome is Pareto efficient when nobody can be made better off without making someone else worse off.
definition: Let $X$ be a [set](c:set) of feasible outcomes, and let each of $n$ agents have a utility [function](c:function) $u_i:X\to\mathbb{R}$ with values in the [real numbers](c:real-number). An outcome $x\in X$ is Pareto efficient if no $y\in X$ has $u_i(y)\ge u_i(x)$ for all $i$ and $u_i(y)>u_i(x)$ for at least one $i$.
examples: When one dollar is split between two people, every split $(a,1-a)$ with $0\le a\le1$ is Pareto efficient.
In the prisoner's dilemma, mutual cooperation is Pareto efficient, although it is not a [Nash equilibrium](c:nash-equilibrium).
Non-example: In the prisoner's dilemma, mutual defection is not Pareto efficient, because both players prefer mutual cooperation.

steps: Write $y\succ x$ when $u_i(y)\ge u_i(x)$ for all $i$ and $u_j(y)>u_j(x)$ for some $j$.
The relation $\succ$ is a strict partial order on the outcomes.
An outcome $x$ is Pareto efficient exactly when no $y$ has $y\succ x$.
That says $x$ is a [maximal element](c:maximal-element) for the order $\succ$.
links.why: Pareto efficient outcomes are the maximal elements of the Pareto order, so tools for maximal elements apply.
